# Results — Study 658 (Put-Write-Premium)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim under test —
**systematically writing cash-secured S&P 500 puts harvests the variance risk premium and
beats buy-and-hold on a risk-adjusted basis** — tested on **PUTW** (WisdomTree CBOE S&P 500
PutWrite Strategy Fund, the only liquid ETF wrapper on the CBOE PUT methodology) against
**SPY**, with **BIL** (T-bill ETF) as the cash leg / risk-free proxy for every excess-of-cash
number. Offline & deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every
number. As-of **2026-06-30** (the last complete calendar month). Fingerprint `3a3191a10828`.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily auto-adjusted (total-return) closes for **PUTW**, **SPY**, **BIL** — 2,601 joint rows, **2016-02-24 → 2026-06-30** (2,600 daily returns) |
| Window | bound by **PUTW's 2016-02-24 inception** — the entire live history of the only tradable product that implements this claim. The CBOE PUT *index* runs back to 1986, but quoting the index instead of the fund would credit a return nobody could actually have banked; the trade-off (a ~9.4-year, single-bull-regime sample) is named, not hidden |
| Cash proxy | **BIL** (1-3 month T-bill ETF) — the risk-free leg for every excess-of-cash Sharpe and HAC test, the same convention as sibling study 655-ivy-portfolio |
| Statistics | Newey-West (HAC, 10 daily lags) *t* on excess-of-cash returns and on the CAPM alpha/beta regression; a crash-day interaction regression (threshold: SPY daily return ≤ −3%, an ex-ante cut, not a sample quantile); a circular block bootstrap (block = 21 trading days ≈ 1 month) on the Sharpe *difference* |
| Execution | **zero look-ahead by construction** — every number is the realized daily return of an already-listed, already-priced ETF; nothing is timed, only held, so there is no signal-to-trade lag to document |
| Costs | already inside PUTW's own NAV (its 0.44% expense ratio, the fund's own monthly-roll execution) — the most honest cost model available, since no assumption is layered on top of what the fund itself already pays away |
| Named crash windows | **"Volmageddon" 2018-01-26 → 2018-02-09** (XIV terminated 2018-02-06) and the **COVID crash 2020-02-19 → 2020-03-23** — hardcoded, conventional peak-to-trough dates, no network |

No survivorship: PUTW and SPY are both live, currently-listed funds over the *entire* window
tested (PUTW's full history, start to as-of) — there is no basket to have survived into.

## The headline — excess-of-cash return, and the CAPM split

| quantity | PUTW | SPY |
|---|--:|--:|
| excess-of-cash return (ann.) | **+6.78%/yr** | **+14.26%/yr** |
| HAC *t* (10 lags) | **+2.00** | **+2.90** |
| Sharpe (excess-of-cash) | **0.53** | **0.80** |
| annualized vol | 12.7% | 17.8% |

| paired comparison | value |
|---|--:|
| PUTW − SPY excess-return gap | **−7.48%/yr**, HAC *t* = **−3.21** |
| Sharpe gap (PUTW − SPY) | **−0.27** — bootstrap 95% CI **[−0.48, −0.00]** (block = 21d, 2,000 draws), PUTW wins the Sharpe race in **2.4%** of draws |

PUTW *does* clear a bare-minimum bar of earning something over cash (*t* = 2.00 — right at,
not comfortably above, the desk's own line), but on the actual question the claim asks —
**does it beat buy-and-hold, risk-adjusted** — the real tape says no, decisively: the excess
gap over SPY is significantly *negative* (*t* = −3.21) and the Sharpe-difference bootstrap
excludes zero on the same side.

## Is the premium just truncated equity beta?

| quantity | value |
|---|--:|
| CAPM alpha (ann., vs SPY) | **−1.78%/yr**, HAC *t* = **−0.95** (not distinguishable from zero) |
| CAPM beta | **0.600**, HAC *t* = **+10.26** |

Once beta is controlled for, there is **no** statistically detectable alpha — the point
estimate is even negative. PUTW's entire average-day behavior is explained by holding roughly
**60% of SPY's market beta**; nothing above that beta is priced in on this tape.

## Does the "lower beta" survive a crash, or widen exactly when it hurts?

| quantity | value |
|---|--:|
| normal-day beta | **0.551**, HAC *t* = **+14.05** |
| extra crash-day beta (SPY ≤ −3% days) | **+0.382**, HAC *t* = **+2.34** |
| implied crash-day beta | **≈ 0.932** |
| crash days in sample | 33 of 2,600 |

The "diversification" is not stable — it is a **regime-dependent** beta. On an ordinary day
PUTW moves about 55% as much as SPY; on the 33 worst days in the sample (SPY down ≥3%) that
slope jumps to **93%**, a statistically significant widening (*t* = 2.34) toward full equity
beta on exactly the days a genuine diversifier is supposed to earn its keep.

## Named crash windows — max drawdown, PUTW vs SPY

| window | PUTW | SPY |
|---|--:|--:|
| Volmageddon 2018-01-26 → 2018-02-09 | **−8.2%** | −10.1% |
| COVID crash 2020-02-19 → 2020-03-23 | **−28.4%** | −33.7% |
| full-sample max drawdown | **−28.4%** | −33.7% |

At first glance PUTW looks protective in both named windows — but that is exactly what a
beta-0.6 asset does in *any* drawdown, crash-conditional widening or not; a shallower
peak-to-trough drawdown here is consistent with (and does not refute) the "it's just beta"
finding above.

## Monthly capture and the tail signature

| quantity | value |
|---|--:|
| monthly up-capture (SPY > 0, n = 89) | **59.3%** |
| monthly down-capture (SPY < 0, n = 35) | **65.8%** |
| worst single month | PUTW **−13.1%** (2020-03) vs SPY −12.5% |
| worst single day | PUTW **−10.51%** vs SPY −10.94% |
| daily skew | PUTW **−1.80** vs SPY −0.32 |

The capture asymmetry (keeps 59% of the up months, gives back 66% of the down months) is the
textbook short-vol shape. And the sharpest data point of all: despite carrying only 71% of
SPY's annualized volatility, PUTW's **single worst month (March 2020, −13.1%) was worse than
SPY's own worst month (−12.5%)** — a smaller-vol asset should not, on average, have a *fatter*
left tail than the benchmark it is a fraction of. That inversion, plus the daily skew of −1.80
(vs SPY's −0.32), is the fingerprint of a truncated-upside, crash-exposed payoff riding on top
of a reduced beta, not a genuine risk-reducer.

## Synthetic positive control — the machinery is unbiased

Deterministic monthly cash-secured-ATM-put engine (Black-Scholes premium), options priced at
`realized_vol × (1 + harvest)`; `harvest = 0` is a "fair" world with **no** embedded volatility
risk premium — the CAPM-alpha detector must not manufacture significance there.

| world | *t*<sub>alpha</sub> | alpha (ann., seed 658 / seed shown) |
|---|--:|--:|
| null (harvest = 0), **20 seeds** | mean **−0.53** (sd 0.98), \|*t*\| ≥ 2 in **1/20 seeds** (≈ the nominal 5% false-positive rate — correctly calibrated, not over- or under-powered) | — |
| planted harvest = +0.25 (seed 658) | **+4.25** | **+4.69%/yr** |

The detector is well-behaved under the null and lights up cleanly on a planted premium.
*(A faithful-engine / power check only — never cited in support of the real-tape stamp.)*

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** PUTW clears only a bare, borderline excess-of-cash return (+6.78%/yr,
  HAC *t* = 2.00 — right at the bar) but the claim under test is "beats buy-and-hold
  risk-adjusted," and the real tape rejects that decisively: paired excess-return gap vs SPY
  **−7.48%/yr at *t* = −3.21**, Sharpe **0.53 vs 0.80** with a bootstrap CI on the gap
  (**[−0.48, −0.00]**) that excludes zero on the losing side, and a CAPM alpha that is
  statistically indistinguishable from zero (*t* = −0.95, point estimate *negative*). Over its
  entire live history the product has **not** delivered the risk-adjusted edge it is sold on.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** There is no residual edge to deploy — what PUTW actually delivers
  is a lower-beta (0.60) equity substitute with a *worse* Sharpe than the index it is priced
  off, whose beta-driven "protection" is not even stable: it widens from 0.55 to **0.93**
  exactly on the worst 33 days in the sample (*t* = 2.34), and its single worst month
  (−13.1%, March 2020) beat SPY's own worst month despite 29% less annualized vol. Costs (the
  fund's own 0.44% expense ratio) are already inside every number above and make no
  difference to the conclusion.
- **"Is it just truncated equity beta?" — CONFIRMED.** Beta 0.60 (*t* = 10.26) explains the
  average day; alpha is statistically zero (*t* = −0.95); and the beta is not even stable —
  it converges toward full equity exposure (≈0.93, *t* = 2.34) on the days a genuine
  diversifier is supposed to prove its worth. There is nothing here beyond a smaller, less
  stable slice of the market it is compared against.
